transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
>> Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Janine Herbst.
The president of Cornell University
says the institution has to do better
following a civil lawsuit filed by a former student
in recent weeks alleging she was gang-raped
at a frat house in 2024.
And Pierce Christian Wright has more.
>> Cornell University President Michael Kotlikoff
says it's a defining moment for the university.
>> What happened to Jane Doe in 2024 is deeply disturbing
and will weigh heavily on our community for years to come.
>> He acknowledges mounting questions over Cornell's handling
of the young woman's rape allegations
and concerns about campus culture.
>> It raises heartbreaking and troubling issues
about sexual assault, dehumanization,
and aspects of party culture, alcohol, and drug use.
>> Cornell's president says the school's taking immediate action
to strengthen sexual assault prevention and education
and substance use resources,
and will take a serious look at the role of fraternities
and sororities in campus life.
He also announced an outside review
into Cornell's handling of the case.
Christian Wright, NPR News.
>> The Supreme Court opens its new term tomorrow
and is set to hear a landmark climate change case
from the city and county of Boulder.
Colorado Public Radio's Ishawn Tokwar has more.
>> In 2018, Boulder sued the oil company's Exxon and Suncor
for damages.
The suit alleges that they lied about the dangers
of burning fossil fuels and should now pitch in
to pay for climate-driven disasters.
Michael Girard is with the Saban Center for Climate Change Law.
>> They're not seeking an order that emissions be reduced
or that less oil and gas and coal be mined or drilled.
They're not seeking emissions regulations.
They're just seeking money damages.
>> The Supreme Court will not rule on the case's merits.
Instead, it's questioning whether Boulder's claims
are trumped by federal law, like the Clean Air Act.
A broad ruling by the court could hamper Boulder's case
and more than two dozen similar climate accountability suits
nationwide.
For NPR News, I'm Ishawn Tokwar in Boulder.
>> U.S. Coast Guard says the search continues
for the people who were on board a Canadian air ambulance
that disappeared off the coast of Massachusetts yesterday.
As NPR's Michelle Aslim reports,
officials are searching a debris field
about 20 miles south of Nantucket.
Search and Mission Coordinator Lieutenant Commander
Castriot Castrati says finding the six people
who were aboard the Gulfstream G-100 jet remains the priority.
>> Because of the amount of debris,
it's very difficult to get into the details of what's there.
But right now, we're really just focused on finding the people.
>> Officials say the waters surrounding the debris field
are around 80 to 90 feet deep.
The twin-engine medical transport plane
was headed from Bermuda to Boston.
Four Canadians and two Bermudans were on board,
and officials say their families have been notified.
Michelle Aslim, NPR News.
>> Most of the Nobel Prize winners will be announced this week.
Tomorrow, the prize in physiology or medicine will be announced.
You're listening to NPR News.
Many churches this weekend are holding their annual
"Blessing of the Animals."
And here's Jason DeRose reports,
it's an opportunity for people of faith
to bring along their pets to worship.
In recent decades, congregations have welcomed pets
not just into the parking lot for the annual blessing,
but into the pews themselves,
like at this Episcopal Church in Ventura, California.
>> Almighty Father, we bless these animals
for all they have done for us.
>> The blessing usually takes place on or near the feast
of St. Francis of Assisi,
the patron saint of animals and the environment.
Among the stories told about Francis
is one in which he preached to birds,
and they too were loved by God.
The blessing of the animals comes at the end
of the new ecumenical season of creation
that many churches are marking for the first time this year.
Jason DeRose, NPR News.
>> At the weekend box office, Amazon, MGM's Verity,
a psychological erotic thriller, took the top spot,
debuting with an estimated $32 million in ticket sales.
But all eyes were on the newly combined
Paramount Warner Brothers Digger,
the Tom Cruise movie that flopped in its opening weekend
with $8 million in ticket sales,
is one of Cruise's worst debuts of his career.
Internationally, where the star is usually a big draw,
the film only made $12 million.
The film cost at least $100 million to produce
with millions more to market it.
I'm Janine Herbst,
And you're listening to NPR News from Washington.

topics.text: Cornell University president says institution must improve after student gang-rape lawsuit filed
Supreme Court begins new term, to hear landmark climate change case from Boulder
U.S. Coast Guard continues search for six people aboard Canadian air ambulance off Massachusetts
Nobel Prize winners announcements begin this week with physiology or medicine prize tomorrow
Many churches hold annual Blessing of the Animals this weekend near feast of St. Francis
Amazon MGM's Verity debuts at weekend box office with estimated $32 million in ticket sales
